lead: A velocity field has two components u and v at every point. Two scalar functions can store that pair. The stream function ψ works for any two-dimensional incompressible flow and gives continuity for free. The velocity potential φ works only when the flow is also irrotational, and gives the velocity as the gradient of a scalar. Engineers use these functions to draw flow nets, compute discharge between streamlines, and solve potential-flow problems around bodies.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the velocity field, Chapter 2.5 for continuity, and Chapter 2.6 for vorticity.

blocks.text: For a two-dimensional flow in the x-y plane, let u be the velocity component in the x direction and v the component in the y direction, both in m/s. Define the stream function ψ(x,y) by u = ∂ψ/∂y and v = −∂ψ/∂x. ψ has units of square metres per second (m²/s), because a velocity in m/s is differentiated with respect to a length in m. The signs are part of the definition; swapping them reverses the flow.

blocks.where: u and v are velocity components in m/s; ψ is the stream function in m²/s; x and y are coordinates in m.

blocks.text: Put these into the continuity equation for steady two-dimensional incompressible flow, ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0. You get ∂²ψ/∂x∂y − ∂²ψ/∂y∂x = 0. The mixed derivatives are equal, so continuity is satisfied automatically. That is why ψ exists for every such flow: pick any smooth ψ and you get a valid incompressible velocity field.

Along a streamline, dψ = (∂ψ/∂x)dx + (∂ψ/∂y)dy = −v dx + u dy. For a streamline, dy/dx = v/u, so dψ = 0. Hence ψ is constant on a streamline. The difference ψ_B − ψ_A between two streamlines is the volume flow rate per unit depth between them, in m²/s. Take the magnitude for discharge; the sign tells the direction. A single stream function needs two-dimensional incompressible flow. A general three-dimensional or compressible flow does not have one scalar ψ that gives both components this way.

When the flow is irrotational, the vorticity is zero everywhere. In two dimensions this means ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y = 0. Then the velocity can be written as the gradient of a scalar φ, called the velocity potential. Use this sign convention: u = −∂φ/∂x and v = −∂φ/∂y. φ has units of m²/s. The minus sign makes the velocity point from high φ to low φ. Keep this convention in every problem; do not switch signs halfway.

blocks.where: φ is the velocity potential in m²/s; u and v are velocity components in m/s; the minus sign is the convention used here.

blocks.text: Lines of constant φ are equipotential lines. Along such a line dφ = −u dx − v dy = 0, so the velocity is perpendicular to the line. Thus equipotential lines cut streamlines at right angles. Because φ exists only for irrotational flow, using φ for a rotational flow is wrong. The stream function can still exist there.

For a two-dimensional incompressible irrotational flow, substitute the definitions into continuity and zero vorticity. For ψ, zero vorticity gives ∂²ψ/∂x² + ∂²ψ/∂y² = 0. For φ, continuity gives ∂²φ/∂x² + ∂²φ/∂y² = 0. Both are Laplace's equation, written ∇²ψ = 0 and ∇²φ = 0. Solutions are called harmonic functions.

items: ψ: exists for 2-D incompressible flow, even if rotational; constant on streamlines; difference gives discharge per unit depth.
φ: exists only for irrotational flow; constant on equipotential lines; lines cross streamlines at 90°.
Use ψ when you need streamlines and discharge; use φ when you need a scalar potential and the flow is irrotational.

figure.caption: A velocity field gives a stream function when the flow is two-dimensional and incompressible, and a velocity potential only when it is also irrotational. The two families of lines meet at right angles.

spec.title: Two functions from one field
spec.aria: One velocity field gives a stream function when the flow is incompressible and a velocity potential when it is irrotational, and their lines cross at right angles.

examples.question: A two-dimensional flow has stream function ψ = x² − y², where ψ is in m²/s and x, y are in metres. (a) Find u and v at the point x = 2 m, y = 3 m. (b) Check continuity at that point. (c) Compute the vorticity and decide whether a velocity potential exists. (d) If it exists, find φ and its value at the same point, taking φ = 0 at the origin.
steps: Differentiate the stream function: u = ∂ψ/∂y = −2y and v = −∂ψ/∂x = −2x. Both are in m/s.
At x = 2 m and y = 3 m: u = −2(3) = −6 m/s and v = −2(2) = −4 m/s.
Continuity: ∂u/∂x = 0 and ∂v/∂y = 0, so ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0 s⁻¹. Continuity holds.
Vorticity: ω_z = ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y = −2 − (−2) = 0 s⁻¹. The flow is irrotational, so φ exists.
For φ: u = −∂φ/∂x = −2y gives ∂φ/∂x = 2y. Integrate in x: φ = 2xy + f(y).
Also v = −∂φ/∂y = −2x gives ∂φ/∂y = 2x. Differentiate φ = 2xy + f(y) with respect to y: 2x + f′(y) = 2x, so f′(y) = 0 and f(y) = C.
Thus φ = 2xy + C. With φ = 0 at the origin, C = 0, so φ = 2xy. At x = 2 m, y = 3 m: φ = 2(2)(3) = 12 m²/s.
Check Laplace: ψ_xx = 2 and ψ_yy = −2, so ψ_xx + ψ_yy = 0. Also φ_xx = 0 and φ_yy = 0, so φ_xx + φ_yy = 0.
examples.answer: At (2 m, 3 m): u = −6 m/s, v = −4 m/s, continuity gives 0 s⁻¹, vorticity is 0 s⁻¹, and φ = 2xy = 12 m²/s.
examples.check:
x = 2.0
y = 3.0
u = -2.0 * y
v = -2.0 * x
continuity = 0.0 + 0.0
vorticity = -2.0 - (-2.0)
phi = 2.0 * x * y
print(u)
print(v)
print(continuity)
print(vorticity)
print(phi)

traps: Using u = ∂ψ/∂x and v = ∂ψ/∂y instead of u = ∂ψ/∂y, v = −∂ψ/∂x. The signs and which derivative go with which component are fixed.
Writing u = +∂φ/∂x in one line and u = −∂φ/∂x in another. Choose the minus convention and keep it.
Assuming every flow has a velocity potential. Rotational flow, such as a forced vortex, has no φ even though it may have a stream function.
Forgetting that ψ in this form needs two-dimensional incompressible flow. A general 3-D flow does not have one scalar ψ.
Giving ψ or φ units of m/s. Both are m²/s.

quiz.q: Define the stream function and give its units.
quiz.a: For 2-D flow, u = ∂ψ/∂y and v = −∂ψ/∂x. ψ is in m²/s.

quiz.q: Why does ψ satisfy continuity automatically?
quiz.a: Substituting u = ψ_y and v = −ψ_x into ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y gives ψ_yx − ψ_xy = 0, because mixed partial derivatives are equal.

quiz.q: For ψ = 3x²y − y³, find u and v at (1 m, 2 m).
A flow has u = 2y and v = 0. Does ψ exist? Does φ exist?
quiz.a: Continuity: ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0 + 0 = 0, so ψ exists. Vorticity: ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y = 0 − 2 = −2 ≠ 0, so the flow is rotational and φ does not exist.

quiz.q: What is the angle between a streamline and an equipotential line?
quiz.a: 90°; the velocity is tangent to the streamline and normal to the equipotential line.

quiz.q: If ψ_A = 0.4 m²/s and ψ_B = 1.0 m²/s on two streamlines, what is the discharge per unit depth between them?
State Laplace's equation for φ and the condition under which it holds.
quiz.a: ∇²φ = ∂²φ/∂x² + ∂²φ/∂y² = 0. It holds for 2-D incompressible irrotational flow.

beyond: Not for the exam. In 2-D irrotational flow, φ and ψ can be combined into a complex potential w = φ + iψ, and complex analysis gives quick solutions for flow around shapes. This is used in aerodynamics and in groundwater seepage models. Modern CFD solves the velocity field directly, but ψ and φ remain useful for checking codes and for teaching. Search for "complex potential", "conformal mapping aerodynamics" and "stream function groundwater".
